location.address: 42nd Street and Park Avenue, Midtown Manhattan

challenge1.keeperOpening: Alright Hunters… here's your first clue. If you figure this out, you will know the location of the first key. The Griffin was seen this morning flying overhead at this location. A place it cares about is waking up — and that means your first Key has appeared.
challenge1.keeperAmusement: Let's see if you can find it.
challenge1.keeperClueDelivery: Here's your first riddle. Don't rush it. Read each line carefully. The Griffin likes details.
challenge1.riddle:
A sky that was painted, not borrowed from night.
A place where the quiet can travel just right.
Four faces agree on the same little tune,
While thousands rush past it from morning till noon.
challenge1.keeperAnswerPrompt: Alright Hunters… what's your answer? Say it clearly so I know you mean it.
challenge1.keeperCorrect: Good. Exactly right. Your first Key is connected to something hidden in this building.
challenge1.keeperIncorrect: Not quite. Think about the stars, the whispers, and the clock. Try again.
challenge1.keeperAfterCorrect: You've solved the first challenge. That's two tokens earned. Head to the landmark when you're ready—the next challenges unlock on the way and when you arrive.
challenge1.keeperTransition: Good work. Now start heading to Grand Central. When you're on your way, say 'Keeper, we're traveling' and I'll give you the next challenge. You'll need what you learn for what comes next.

fragmentPuzzle.keeperInstructions: These letters were found near the landmark. One doesn't belong — it's just there to throw you off. Unscramble the rest to find the word.
fragmentPuzzle.content: G R A N D C E N T R A L X

challenge2.keeperOpening: Since you're on your way, learn a bit about where you're going. These questions will help you later. Don't rush them. Answer each one carefully. Each correct answer earns you one token.

questions.question: What year did Grand Central Terminal officially open?
questions.keeperHint: Michelin NYC Guide - page 180. It was opened 10 years after it was designed
questions.keeperIncorrect: Not quite. Try again.

questions.question: What material is the main concourse floor made from?
questions.keeperHint: NYC Landmarks - page 103.

questions.question: The main ceiling shows zodiac constellations. Why do you think the designers chose to include stars instead of a regular painted ceiling?
questions.keeperHint: There's no single right answer here. Think about what the stars might represent. What feeling were they trying to create?
questions.answer: To create a sense of wonder
acceptableAnswers: To create a sense of wonder
to connect the station to the sky
choices: Because the original architect had a degree in astronomy
To create a sense of wonder and inspire travelers
To follow a city law requiring art in public buildings
To make the ceiling look higher than it actually is

questions.question: What is the name of the famous spot where people can hear each other whisper from across the room?
questions.keeperHint: Lonely Planet NYC Guide - Page 185.

questions.question: The constellations on the ceiling are reversed. What is the most common explanation people give for why they're backwards?
questions.keeperHint: Lonely Planet NYC Guide - Page 185.
choices: The paint dried before it could be corrected
A perspective from God's view, looking down
The original blueprint was printed in reverse
The artist copied a medieval star map by accident

questions.question: Why do you think the designers placed the famous brass clock at the exact center of the main concourse?
questions.keeperHint: Think about what a clock does. Why put it where everyone can see it?
questions.answer: To serve as a meeting point that every traveler could spot
acceptableAnswers: To help travelers know the time
to serve as a meeting point
choices: To serve as a meeting point that every traveler could spot
Because that was the only spot with enough floor space
To mark the center for the building's structural balance
To honor the Vanderbilt family tradition of clockmaking

questions.question: At its peak in 1947, how many people used Grand Central Terminal in a single year?
questions.keeperHint: Michelin NYC Guide - page 180.

questions.question: The large sculpture above Grand Central's main entrance is called 'The Glory of Commerce.' Which Roman god stands at the center of it?
questions.keeperHint: Michelin NYC Guide - page 180.

questions.question: Grand Central Terminal has been called the 'Gateway to the ___.' What word completes that phrase?
questions.keeperHint: Michelin NYC Guide - page 180.

questions.question: There's a small dark patch on the ceiling that was left uncleaned on purpose. What does it show?
questions.keeperHint: This connects to what you'll need to find later. What was the ceiling like before it was cleaned?
questions.answer: How dirty the ceiling used to be from smoke
choices: Where a skylight was removed decades ago
How dirty the ceiling used to be from smoke
An old mural that was painted over during renovation
Where a section of plaster collapsed and was patched

challenge2.keeperCompletion: Alright. You've got the important pieces. Remember what you learned — especially about that ceiling detail. When you arrive at Grand Central, say 'Keeper, we are here' and I'll give you the final challenge. And remember: most people never look up.

challenge3.keeperOpening: Good. You made it. Look up at the ceiling. Most people never notice what the Griffin spotted years ago.
challenge3.clue:
Somewhere on the main concourse ceiling, there is a small dark patch that was left uncleaned on purpose.
Find it and tell me what it's called.
challenge3.keeperInstructions: Look up at the main concourse ceiling. Find the one small patch that's darker than everything around it — left that way on purpose. Tell me what you'd call it.

hints.text: Look up at the ceiling near the northwest corner. It's darker than the rest — left that way on purpose to show what the whole ceiling used to look like before restoration.

challenge3.keeperProofPrompt: What is the dark spot on the ceiling called?
challenge3.keeperCorrect: That's it. Left there on purpose — a reminder of what the whole ceiling looked like before it was cleaned. Good eye, Hunters.
challenge3.keeperIncorrect: Look up. There's one small spot on the ceiling that's darker than everything around it. What would you call it?
challenge3.keeperCompletion:
That patch was left on purpose — a quiet reminder of how the station looked before it was restored. The Griffin noticed it years ago. And now you have too.

The Key for this landmark is yours. Claim it and choose your next destination when you're ready.

keyRiddle.keeperOpening: You've done well. Now one last puzzle before you claim the Key. Think about everything you learned today — especially what stands at the center of this place.
keyRiddle.riddle:
Four faces watch, though none have eyes.
They tick in opal, never surprise.
Where thousands pass and ask their way,
The Key is waiting there today.
keyRiddle.keeperAnswerPrompt: Where is the Key hidden? Name the spot.
keyRiddle.keeperCorrect: That's it. The Information Booth — the four-faced opal clock right at the center of the main concourse. Go there now.
keyRiddle.keeperIncorrect: Think about what stands at the very center of the main concourse. What do people gather around when they need directions — or when they're meeting someone?
keyRiddle.keeperFinal: The Key is waiting at the Information Booth. The famous four-faced opal clock marks the spot. Go claim your first Key.

challenge1.keeperOpening: Good work on the first Key, Hunters. The Griffin was spotted again — circling a building not far from where you started. Quiet on the outside, enormous on the inside. It's been watching this place for years. Your second Key has appeared.
challenge1.keeperAmusement: This one requires a careful reader.
challenge1.keeperClueDelivery: Here's your second riddle. Take your time with it.
challenge1.riddle:
Two stone guards watch over a stair that rises slow.
The doors hold everything you need to know.
A painted sky hangs quiet above long rows of light,
While seven floors of stories sleep just out of sight.
challenge1.keeperAnswerPrompt: What's your answer, Hunters? Say it clearly.
challenge1.keeperCorrect: Good. That's the one. Most people walk right past those lions without knowing their names. Your second Key is connected to something hidden inside.
challenge1.keeperIncorrect: Not quite. Think about the lions. Think about what's inside. What do you do there? Try again.
challenge1.keeperAfterCorrect: Two tokens earned. Head to the library when you're ready — the next challenge unlocks on the way, and when you arrive there's one final riddle to find the Key.
challenge1.keeperTransition: Start walking to the library on 5th Avenue at 42nd Street. When you're on your way, say 'Keeper, we're traveling' and I'll give you the next challenge.

challenge2.keeperOpening: Since you're on your way, let's make the walk useful. These questions will help you when you arrive. Answer carefully. Each correct answer earns a token.

questions.question: What year did the New York Public Library's main branch open?
questions.keeperHint: It opened two years before Grand Central Terminal.
questions.keeperIncorrect: Not quite. Think about the early twentieth century.

questions.question: What are the names of the two lion statues at the front entrance?
questions.keeperHint: A mayor gave them their names during the Great Depression.
questions.keeperCorrect: Patience and Fortitude. Exactly. One token.
questions.keeperIncorrect: Look up who named the lions and when.

questions.question: Which New York City mayor gave the lions their names?
questions.keeperHint: He was mayor during the Great Depression. There's a major New York airport named after him.
questions.keeperIncorrect: Think about the airport named after a famous New York mayor.

questions.question: The library was built by combining three private collections. Why do you think a public library needed private donors instead of just city funding?
questions.keeperHint: Think about who had the most books and money in the 1890s, and what the city could or couldn't afford.
questions.answer: Private collections and funding were needed because the city couldn't afford to build such a large collection on its own
choices: Because the city was at war and couldn't spend money on books
Because wealthy donors already had the collections and the city lacked both funds and materials
Because private libraries were cheaper to build than public ones
Because the city council voted against using public funds
questions.keeperIncorrect: Think about who had books and money in New York in the 1890s.

questions.question: How many floors underground are the library's book stacks?
questions.keeperHint: There's a lot of space you can't see from the street.
questions.keeperCorrect: Seven floors underground. Correct. One token.
questions.keeperIncorrect: Think bigger. There's a lot of Manhattan underground.

questions.question: The famous Rose Main Reading Room has a painted ceiling. What does it depict?
questions.keeperHint: Think about what you'd see if the ceiling were actually a window to the outside.
choices: A map of Manhattan from above
A cloudy sky with warm light
questions.keeperCorrect: Right. A painted sky. Remember that detail — you'll need it later.
questions.keeperIncorrect: Think about what's usually above you when you're outside.

questions.question: What architectural firm designed the library building? (Hint: it was a two-person partnership)
questions.keeperHint: Search for 'New York Public Library architects.' Different architects than Grand Central.
questions.keeperCorrect: Carrère and Hastings. Right. One token.
questions.keeperIncorrect: Look it up. Different architects than Grand Central.

questions.question: The three founding collections came from Astor and Lenox — who was the third founding family?
questions.keeperHint: Their name is part of the library's full official title.
questions.keeperIncorrect: Their name is still in the library's full official name.

questions.question: When you walk into the first hall — called Astor Hall — what material are the floor, walls, and arched ceiling made from?
questions.keeperHint: Think about polished, expensive building materials used in grand New York buildings.
questions.keeperIncorrect: Same material as parts of Grand Central. Think polished and white.

questions.question: The Rose Main Reading Room was closed for years and reopened in 2016 after restoration. What caused the damage?
questions.keeperHint: Think about what happens to painted ceilings in old buildings when they aren't maintained.
questions.answer: Water damage had deteriorated the painted ceiling and plaster
choices: A fire had damaged parts of the upper floors
Water damage had deteriorated the painted ceiling and plaster
The original architect's design had structural flaws
City code violations required complete interior redesign
questions.keeperCorrect: Right. Water damage. Remember what you learned about that ceiling — you'll need it soon.
questions.keeperIncorrect: Think about what typically damages painted ceilings in old buildings over many decades.

challenge2.keeperCompletion: Good. You've got the important pieces. Remember what you learned — especially about that painted ceiling. When you arrive at the library, say 'Keeper, we are here' and I'll give you the final challenge.

challenge3.keeperOpening: Good. You made it. Those lions have been sitting there for over a hundred years. The Griffin thinks they're amateurs. There's something about this building most visitors miss because they're too excited to get inside. Stop before you go through the doors.
challenge3.clue:
Stand at the top of the front steps before going inside.
Look up at the inscription carved in the stone above the central entrance.
Three founding family names are carved there — the people who made this library possible.
Find the name that comes first when you put all three in alphabetical order.
That same name appears again on the first hall you'll walk through when you go inside.
Tell me that name.
challenge3.keeperInstructions: Read the inscription carefully. The three names are all there. Sort them alphabetically and tell me which comes first. Then go inside and find the hall that shares that name.

hints.text: The three founding families are Astor, Lenox, and Tilden. Their names are carved into the stone above the main entrance.
Alphabetical order: which of the three names — Astor, Lenox, or Tilden — comes first when sorted like a dictionary?

Astor comes first alphabetically. Look above the main entrance for the three family names. Then walk inside — the first hall you enter is named after that same family. It's a marble hall with a vaulted ceiling.

challenge3.keeperProofPrompt: What family name comes first alphabetically in the inscription — and what is the first hall inside named?
challenge3.keeperCorrect: Astor. Right. Their collection started all of this. And you're standing in Astor Hall. Good eyes, Hunters.
challenge3.keeperIncorrect: Read the inscription above the central entrance. Find the three family names and sort them alphabetically. Which one comes first?
challenge3.keeperCompletion:
Well done. Most people walk straight through that hall without reading a word of it. The Griffin has always stopped to read it.

You've completed all three challenges. One last riddle stands between you and the Key. Solve it and you'll know exactly where to go.

keyRiddle.keeperOpening: You've earned your way inside. One last puzzle before you claim the Key. Think about the ceiling you learned about — and the flower in its name.
keyRiddle.riddle:
No sun shines here, no rain comes through,
Yet clouds drift softly in your view.
Named for a bloom, it holds long rows of light.
Go find the room — the Key's in sight.
keyRiddle.keeperAnswerPrompt: Where is the Key hidden? Name the room.
keyRiddle.keeperCorrect: The Rose Main Reading Room. Exactly. Third floor, north end. Go claim your Key.
keyRiddle.keeperIncorrect: Think about the room with the painted cloudy sky. It's named after a flower. What flower?
keyRiddle.keeperFinal: The Key is waiting in the Rose Main Reading Room. Head up to the third floor, walk to the north end, and look at the carved wooden panels below the arched windows. Your second Key is there. Go get it.

challenge1.keeperOpening: Good work, Hunters. The Griffin has been spotted out in the harbor — circling something that stands in the water but never gets its feet wet. It's been watching this one from the air for a long time. Your third Key has appeared.
challenge1.keeperAmusement: This one came a long way.
challenge1.keeperClueDelivery: Here's your third riddle. Read it out loud if it helps.
challenge1.riddle:
A gift that crossed the ocean, she stands in the bay.
Her arm's been held up since the gift-giving day.
What once shone like a penny now shows only green —
Count the points on her crown: seven seas in between.
challenge1.keeperAnswerPrompt: What's your answer, Hunters? Say it clearly.
challenge1.keeperCorrect: Good. That's the one. Most people only look at her face and the torch. Your third Key is connected to something most visitors miss entirely.
challenge1.keeperIncorrect: Not quite. Think about where you can see water on all sides, and something very tall standing in the middle of it. Try again.
challenge1.keeperAfterCorrect: Two tokens earned. Head to the ferry terminal when you're ready — the next challenge unlocks on the way, and when you arrive there's one final riddle to find the Key.
challenge1.keeperTransition: Make your way to the ferry at Battery Park. When you're on your way, say 'Keeper, we're traveling' and I'll give you the next challenge.

fragmentPuzzle.keeperInstructions: These letters were found near the landmark. One doesn't belong — it's just there to throw you off. Unscramble the rest to find the word.
fragmentPuzzle.content: S T A T U E O F L I B E R T Y X

challenge2.keeperOpening: The ferry ride is a good time to learn a few things. These questions will help you when you arrive. Answer carefully. Each correct answer earns a token.

questions.question: What year was the Statue of Liberty officially dedicated?
questions.keeperHint: It was dedicated ten years after America's centennial — the 100th anniversary of independence.
questions.keeperIncorrect: Think about ten years after America's hundredth birthday.

questions.question: Which country gave the Statue of Liberty as a gift to the United States?
questions.keeperHint: Think about which European country sided with America during the Revolutionary War.
questions.keeperIncorrect: Think about which country helped America during the Revolution. They've been close allies ever since.

questions.question: What material was used to build the outer shell of the Statue of Liberty?
questions.keeperHint: It's the same metal used in old pennies — and it changes color when it weathers.
questions.keeperIncorrect: Think about old pennies — same color when new. Same metal.

questions.question: When the statue was built, it was a shiny reddish-brown color. Now it's green. Why do you think copper turns green over time?
questions.keeperHint: Think about what happens to metal left outside in the rain and air for a very long time.
questions.answer: A chemical reaction between the copper and oxygen and water in the air, called oxidation
choices: Someone painted it green to match the harbor
A chemical reaction between the copper, air, and water called oxidation
It absorbed color from the ocean water over many decades
The metal slowly changed color from reflecting the sky on cloudy days
questions.keeperCorrect: Right. Oxidation. The copper reacted with the air and water. One token.
questions.keeperIncorrect: Think about what happens to other metals left outside in the weather. What do you call it when metal changes from a reaction with air and water?

questions.question: How many rays are on the crown of the Statue of Liberty, and what do they represent?
questions.keeperHint: Count the number of continents in the world. That's the same number as the rays.
questions.answer: 7 rays representing the 7 seas and 7 continents
choices: 5 rays for the five boroughs of New York City
7 rays for the 7 seas and 7 continents
10 rays for the Bill of Rights
questions.keeperCorrect: Seven. Right. Seas and continents. One token.
questions.keeperIncorrect: Count the continents on a map. That's your clue.

questions.question: Who designed and sculpted the Statue of Liberty?
questions.keeperHint: He was a French sculptor. His last name starts with B.
questions.keeperIncorrect: He was French. Look him up — his last name starts with B.

questions.question: Which famous engineer built the internal iron framework that holds the statue upright — and also later built the most famous tower in France?
questions.keeperHint: Think about the most famous tower in Paris. Who built it?
questions.keeperCorrect: Eiffel. Same person, same style of iron framework. One token.
questions.keeperIncorrect: Think about the Eiffel Tower. Who built it? Same person built the inside of this statue.

questions.question: There is something unusual at the feet of the Statue of Liberty that most visitors never notice. What is it?
questions.keeperHint: Most people only look up at her face and torch. Look down — at what she's stepping over.
choices: A pile of coins from different countries
A broken chain symbolizing freedom from oppression
A map of the world carved into the stone base
A plaque listing the names of immigrants
questions.keeperCorrect: A broken chain. She's walking away from it. Remember that detail — you'll need it later.
questions.keeperIncorrect: Most people are looking up. You need to look down — at what she's leaving behind as she walks.

questions.question: The tablet in the statue's left hand has a date written in Roman numerals. What date does it show?
questions.keeperHint: Think about the most important date in American history — the day the country declared independence.
choices: January 1, 1776 — the start of the Revolution
questions.keeperCorrect: July 4, 1776. Independence Day. Right. One token.
questions.keeperIncorrect: Think about the most important date in American history. When did the country declare independence?

questions.question: A poem called 'The New Colossus' is displayed inside the pedestal of the Statue of Liberty. What is the most famous line from it?
questions.keeperHint: It starts with 'Give me your...' and is about welcoming people from other countries.
questions.answer: Give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free
acceptableAnswers: give me your tired your poor
choices: Give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free
Let freedom ring from the mountaintops of every state
We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal
With liberty and justice for all who cross beneath her flame
questions.keeperCorrect: Right. That's the line. You'll find the plaque when you arrive. One token.
questions.keeperIncorrect: It starts with 'Give me your...' — think about what the statue is welcoming people toward.

challenge2.keeperCompletion: Good. You know what to look for now. When you get off the ferry and reach the statue, say 'Keeper, we are here' and I'll give you the final challenge. Remember: most people only look up.

challenge3.keeperOpening: Good. You made it to the island. The Griffin has been perching out here for years — it likes the harbor view. There's something at the base of the statue that most visitors never notice. Time to fix that.
challenge3.clue:
Walk around the base of the statue and look down at her feet.
She's not just standing still — she's walking.
Most visitors are too busy looking up at her face and torch to notice.
Find what she left behind, and tell me what it is.
challenge3.keeperInstructions: Walk slowly around the statue base. Look at the ground near her feet. Don't rush.

hints.text: She's stepping over something. Look at what's on the ground at her right foot — it's made of metal links.
The links used to be connected. They're not anymore. Look for what's broken.
There's a broken chain beneath her right foot. She's stepping over it and walking away. It represents freedom from slavery and oppression. That's what you're looking for.

challenge3.keeperProofPrompt: What's at the feet of the statue — and what do you think it means?
challenge3.keeperCorrect: A broken chain. She stepped over it and kept walking. Most people never look down long enough to see it. Good eyes.
challenge3.keeperIncorrect: You're in the right area. Walk slowly around the base and look at the ground near her feet. Something's down there that she left behind.
challenge3.keeperCompletion:
You found what most people miss. The Griffin noticed it years ago — made sense to something that knows what it means to be free.

All three challenges done. One last riddle before you claim the Key. Solve it and you'll know where to go.

keyRiddle.keeperOpening: One last puzzle. Think about the poem you learned about — and what it says to people arriving for the very first time.
keyRiddle.riddle:
No tongue, but she speaks to the ones who've crossed the sea.
Her words live in the stone below — a promise to the free.
Find the plaque that starts with 'Give' — it's cut from bronze, not bone.
The Key is resting near the place where her welcome was first shown.
keyRiddle.keeperAnswerPrompt: Where is the Key hidden? Name the spot.
keyRiddle.keeperCorrect: The New Colossus plaque. Inside the pedestal. That's it. Go find it.
keyRiddle.keeperIncorrect: Think about the poem you learned. It's not outside — you have to go inside the pedestal to find it. Where is it displayed?
keyRiddle.keeperFinal: The Key is waiting near the New Colossus plaque inside the pedestal. Go claim your third Key.
